lead.headline: Google replaces Flash with Gemini 4 Hydrogen as Nvidia's chief resigns
lead.dek: DeepMind uses AI agents to prove parts of Signal's encryption, TSMC lines up a billion dollars for OpenAI and Anthropic, and GitHub explains how to write an agent skill that lasts.

bottom_line: Google rolled out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which replaces Gemini 3.8 Flash across its products and is available immediately; Google claims it is 2.5 times faster in high thinking mode and makes far fewer fabricated claims. Nvidia's board said Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, effective immediately. Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to formally verify key guarantees of the Signal protocol in four weeks. TSMC's board approved up to 500 million dollars each for OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Reuters. For builders, GitHub published a practical guide to agent skills, and United Airlines said it will block AI agents from managing bookings.

explainer.title: What formal verification is, and why AI changes the cost
explainer.text:
Formal verification means proving, with mathematics, that a system does what its specification says. Wikipedia's definition is the act of proving or disproving the correctness of a system with respect to a formal specification or property, using formal methods.

That is different from testing. A test checks the cases you thought of. A proof covers every case the specification describes. Ars Technica notes that proponents have long called it a holy grail of software security for that reason.

The catch has always been labor. People had to describe the properties they wanted, turn them into formulas, and then build the proof, which Ars calls incredibly time-consuming. Agentic AI cuts the time of that last part, which is how DeepMind checked key guarantees of the Signal protocol in four weeks. The work was limited in scope: it did not verify the whole Signal app.

playbook.title: Write an agent skill once and reuse it on any agent
playbook.who: Andrea Griffiths, GitHub, with Shishir Tewari, senior manager of data engineering at Procore
playbook.summary: A skill is a versioned folder built around a SKILL.md file that says when and how to do one repeatable task. It carries instructions, not access: the environment still has to supply the tools, credentials and permissions. Use it for bounded, repeatable work such as a checklist, release, migration or metric pipeline.
steps: Give each skill one clear job with a defined input and output, and say in the file when it applies.
Do not let an agent grade its own work. Use a separate verifier skill that checks the changes and shows evidence.
For bigger workflows, split the work into several skills with one responsibility each, and have them share project context instead of rediscovering it.
Keep project names, databases and conventions in a separate manifest file, not hardcoded in the skill.
If the workflow needs shared state, an audit trail, long-running control or enforced permissions, build an application instead.

playbook.title: Put the agent's long pull request description behind a fold
playbook.who: Simon Willison, developer and author of Simon Willison's Weblog
playbook.summary: Agent-written pull request descriptions are accurate and thorough, and readers skip them because they read like filler. His fix keeps all of it but leads with a short introduction a person chose, so a reviewer gets the point at a glance and can expand the rest.
steps: Open the pull request with the shortest human-approved paragraph that gets a reader up to speed. Add a screenshot when it helps.
Wrap the full agent-written description in details and summary tags, which GitHub Markdown renders as a collapsed section.
Use the model name, and the effort level if you set one, as the summary line so it is obvious who wrote the hidden part.

playbook.title: Treat agent work as four stages: plan, build, verify, observe
playbook.who: Nick Liffen and Philip Holleran, GitHub
playbook.summary: GitHub's guide argues that faster code generation moves the pressure elsewhere, citing a Faros AI study in which pull requests spent 441 percent longer in review as teams adopted AI heavily. Its answer is to use agents across the whole job, not only for writing code.
steps: Plan first: gather the scattered context, such as the design, the requirement buried in chat and the old pull request, into one place before writing anything.
Have the agent compare approaches and turn the decisions into a written implementation plan the team agrees on.
Carry the same plan through build, verify and observe, so review and production checks are part of the work and not an afterthought.

playbook.title: From March: split long builds across a planner, a generator and an evaluator
playbook.summary: An older piece that is still the clearest description of the pattern. For multi-hour autonomous coding, a single agent tends to go off the rails. Separating planning, building and grading, with a critic that judges against written criteria, produced complete applications.
steps: Turn subjective goals into concrete, gradable criteria before you ask anything to judge the output.
Break the build into tractable chunks and pass structured artifacts between sessions to carry context.
Read the model's traces on realistic problems and tune from what you see.
When a new model arrives, re-examine the harness and strip out the parts that no longer improve results.

front.summary: Google had the busiest day of the labs, with a new default model and a research result on Signal. The money and hardware story ran through Nvidia's boardroom and TSMC's, while governments and companies kept deciding where AI agents are and are not welcome.

axes.name: Google
axes.text: Gemini 4 Hydrogen replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across Google's products with access open immediately, unlike the staged Argon and Carbon releases. It runs at four thinking levels including a new xhigh. A newsletter also reports Google launched Gemini Decision 1, a low-cost decision model, at an engineering conference.

axes.name: Google DeepMind
axes.text: Researchers used agentic AI and a new framework called AlphaProof Code to formally verify a number of the Signal protocol's key cryptographic guarantees in a four-week proof-of-concept. Ars Technica notes the scope was limited and that it is unclear how practical the approach is for large amounts of code.

axes.name: Anthropic
axes.text: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9. It says they are the same underlying model, with Fable carrying cybersecurity and biology safeguards. TSMC plans to buy Anthropic common shares at the expected price of its public offering.

axes.name: OpenAI
axes.text: OpenAI said more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a free year of ChatGPT Plus in the past year, and that it has run more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community with seven more scheduled this year.

axes.name: Chips: Nvidia and TSMC
axes.text: Nvidia's board announced Jensen Huang's resignation as president, chief executive and director. TSMC's board approved up to 500 million dollars of OpenAI preferred stock and 500 million of Anthropic shares, Reuters reported; analysts quoted by Ars warned about circular financing among investors, suppliers and customers.

axes.name: Government and schools
axes.text: The FAA expanded an AI tool that advises air traffic controllers to the whole national airspace; the controllers' union says it was not involved in designing or testing it. Families protested in seven US cities against Google's AI in schools after Google confirmed students cannot use Search without AI.

axes.name: Agents meet the real world
axes.text: United Airlines will block AI agents from managing reservations and purchases, citing security, privacy and legal risks from shared logins. Fireworks AI, a platform for running open models, confirmed a breach that exposed customer data including Notion users' chat transcripts.

sections.summary: Google's new default model is the day's release. Anthropic's latest pair from earlier in the week is included for reference, with its date.

items.headline: Gemini 4 Hydrogen takes over from Flash across Google's products
items.summary: Hydrogen is the faster, cheaper tier most people in Google's ecosystem use, and it is available at once instead of in stages. It offers four thinking levels, including a new xhigh. Google's own analysis claims it is 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8 in high mode and cuts fabricated claims by more than five times.

items.headline: Google launches a low-cost decision model, a newsletter reports
items.summary: Latent Space reports that Google announced Gemini Decision 1 at the AI Engineer conference: a calibrated multimodal decision model that takes up to 1,000 questions, costs ten cents per million input tokens and responds in about 200 milliseconds. The newsletter adds the usual caveat about benchmarks.

items.headline: From November 9: Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
items.summary: Older than today's window. Anthropic says the two are the same underlying model, with Fable carrying strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards so it can be made more widely available. It reports improvements in coding, reasoning and vision.

sections.summary: Two findings: AI agents helping to prove that encryption works as designed, and a study on chatbots sending shoppers to risky sites.

items.headline: DeepMind uses AI agents to formally verify parts of the Signal protocol
items.summary: In a four-week proof-of-concept, researchers proved a number of the protocol's key cryptographic guarantees using a new framework called AlphaProof Code. Ars Technica calls it further independent validation of encryption used by Signal, Google Messages and WhatsApp, and notes the analysis did not cover the whole Signal app.

items.headline: Study: chatbots showed risky shopping links in up to 15 percent of conversations
items.summary: A study by the IP protection firm Podqi, shared with The Verge, tested Gemini, Perplexity and ChatGPT and found that shoppers could be directed to imposter and other risky websites. This is one firm's study.

sections.summary: For people who build with these tools, the news was about where agents are allowed to act and what happens to the data they touch. The how-to material is in the Playbook below.

items.headline: United Airlines will block AI agents from managing bookings
items.summary: The airline cited cybersecurity, privacy and legal risks when customers hand their logins to third-party agents. The Record notes Bank of America warned customers last week never to share IDs and passwords with agents, and that companies are struggling to tell customers from their assistants.

items.headline: Breach at Fireworks AI exposes customers' data
items.summary: Fireworks AI, which developers use to run open models, confirmed an attacker breached its cloud provider to reach a development system and took billing information and some datasets. Notion disclosed that its customers' chat transcripts were accessed. Fireworks lists Harvey and Cursor among its customers.

items.headline: From November 6: GitHub counts 1.2 billion commits in one week
items.summary: Older than today's window. GitHub says commits in one October week were more than 400 percent above a year earlier and more than it received in all of 2025. The same post cites a Faros AI study in which pull requests spent 441 percent longer in review as teams adopted AI heavily.

sections.summary: A leadership shock at the company whose chips power the field, a chipmaker buying into two labs, and governments and families pushing in opposite directions on deployment.

items.headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia's chief executive
items.summary: The board said Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately, after 33 years, with Colette Kress as interim replacement. TechCrunch reports he stepped down after reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, and that he has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving.

items.headline: TSMC to invest up to a billion dollars in OpenAI and Anthropic
items.summary: TSMC's board approved up to 500 million dollars of OpenAI preferred stock and 500 million of Anthropic common shares at the expected price of its public offering, according to Reuters. Analysts warned that this kind of circular financing among investors, suppliers and customers carries risk.

items.headline: FAA extends AI advice for controllers to the whole country
items.summary: The 875 million dollar SMART system advises air traffic controllers on rerouting. The FAA says it has helped reroute 180 flights over Washington since September 21, saving about 10 minutes and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight. The controllers' union says it had no part in designing or testing it.

items.headline: Families in seven cities protest Google's AI in schools
items.summary: The protests followed Google's confirmation that students cannot use Search without AI. Google said it was giving schools more choice by turning Search, Gemini and Gemini Notebook off by default, but it offers no option for Search without AI.

items.headline: OpenAI says 20,000 veterans and servicemembers took its free year of ChatGPT Plus
items.summary: The offer is for transitioning servicemembers and veterans. OpenAI says its academy and partners have held more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, with seven more scheduled before the end of the year.

items.headline: Finland and Estonia want an EU plan for serious AI incidents
items.summary: In a letter seen by Politico, the two countries say the EU can still compete at the frontier of AI but must govern it responsibly. AI safety and security are on the agenda of Friday's European Council meeting, the first devoted to AI.

upcoming.title: European Council meets on AI
upcoming.detail: The first leaders' meeting devoted to AI, with safety and security on the agenda.

upcoming.title: Huang due to testify by Thanksgiving
upcoming.detail: The former Nvidia chief agreed to appear before Congress by the holiday after lawmakers threatened a subpoena.

audio.script:
This is the A I Dispatch for Thursday, November twelfth.

Here is the bottom line. Google has replaced its Flash model with a new one called Gemini four Hydrogen, and it is available to everyone right away. Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, has resigned. Google DeepMind used A I agents to mathematically prove parts of the encryption behind Signal. And the chipmaker T S M C is putting up to a billion dollars into Open A I and Anthropic.

Start with the models. Gemini four Hydrogen is the faster, cheaper tier that most people in Google's products use. Unlike Google's last two releases, it was not staged. It runs at four thinking levels, including a new one called extra high. Google's own analysis claims it is two and a half times faster than the model it replaces, even in high mode, and that it makes five times fewer fabricated claims. Those are the company's numbers.

A newsletter, Latent Space, also reports that Google launched a low cost decision model called Gemini Decision one at an engineering conference. Treat that as one outlet's report. And for reference, from November ninth, Anthropic released Claude Fable five point two and Claude Mythos five point two. Anthropic says they are the same underlying model, and that Fable carries safeguards for cybersecurity and biology.

On to research. Google DeepMind researchers used agentic A I, and a new framework called Alpha Proof Code, to formally verify a number of the Signal protocol's key guarantees. They did it in four weeks. Ars Technica notes the limits. The work did not cover the whole Signal app, and it is not yet clear how practical this is for large amounts of code. Separately, a study shared with The Verge found that chatbots showed risky shopping links in as many as fifteen percent of conversations. That is one firm's study.

For people who build with these tools. United Airlines says it will block A I agents from managing bookings, because customers are handing those agents their logins. And Fireworks A I, a platform for running open models, confirmed a breach. The attacker took billing information and some datasets, and Notion says its customers' chat transcripts were accessed.

In industry and policy. Nvidia's board says Jensen Huang has resigned as chief executive, effective immediately, after thirty three years. He has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. T S M C's board approved up to five hundred million dollars for Open A I and the same for Anthropic, according to Reuters. Analysts warn about money circling between investors, suppliers and customers. The F A A has expanded an A I tool that advises air traffic controllers to the whole country. The controllers' union says it was not involved in designing or testing it. Families in seven American cities protested Google's A I in schools. Open A I says more than twenty thousand veterans and transitioning servicemembers have claimed a free year of Chat G P T Plus. And Finland and Estonia want the European Union to have a plan for serious A I incidents, ahead of tomorrow's leaders' meeting on A I.

Now the playbook. Four techniques from people who build these tools.

One. Write an agent skill once and reuse it. This comes from Andrea Griffiths at GitHub. A skill is a folder built around one file that says when and how to do a repeatable task. Give each skill one clear job. Do not let an agent grade its own work; use a separate verifier. Keep project names and settings in a separate file, not inside the skill. And remember a skill carries instructions, not access.

Two. Hide the agent's long pull request description behind a fold. This is from Simon Willison. Agents write accurate, thorough descriptions that nobody reads. So open with a short paragraph a person chose, then tuck the full text into a collapsed section, labelled with the model that wrote it.

Three. Treat agent work as four stages: plan, build, verify and observe. This is from two GitHub engineers. Their point is that faster code moves the pressure to review. So gather the scattered context first, have the agent compare approaches, and write the plan down before any code.

Four, from March, and still worth knowing. For long autonomous builds, split the work across a planner, a generator and an evaluator. This is from Prithvi Rajasekaran at Anthropic. Turn fuzzy goals into criteria that can be graded. Break the build into chunks. Read what the model actually did. And when a new model arrives, strip out the parts of your setup that no longer help.

Learn one thing today. Formal verification means proving with mathematics that a system does what its specification says. A test checks the cases you thought of. A proof covers every case the specification describes. The catch has always been the labor of building the proof. A I agents cut that time, which is how DeepMind checked Signal in four weeks.

In the days ahead, European leaders meet on A I tomorrow, and Jensen Huang is due before Congress by Thanksgiving.

That is the A I Dispatch. Every item is linked to its source on the page.
